sections.title: Chapter One - Bunnies, Bells, and Babies
sections.html:
CHAPTER ONE

Bunnies, Bells, and Babies


YOU EVER WONDER what rabbits and brightly colored eggs have to do with a crucified carpenter from 2,000 years ago?

No?

That’s okay. Nobody else does either.

But you should, because it’s hilarious.

See, if you were raised with Easter baskets and pastel decorations, odds are no one sat you down and explained how a fertility goddess ended up hopping across your breakfast table in a felt costume.

And if they did, they probably said something like:
“Oh, it's about Jesus coming back to life, sweetie. Now go find that plastic egg full of Skittles.”

Let’s take a little trip.

The rabbit, or hare, originally, was a symbol of fertility.
Why?

Because rabbits do what rabbits do best: they screw like crazy.

Ancient Europeans knew this. So when spring came, the season of renewal, birth, and planting, they didn’t break out a Bible. They broke out the rabbits.

Spring festivals across Germanic and Anglo-Saxon cultures may have honored Ēostre, a goddess of fertility and dawn. Yes, Easter might gets its name from her.

So what did they do?

They celebrated the Earth waking back up.
They painted eggs (symbols of fertility and new life).
They probably drank beer and danced barefoot in a meadow.
And they honored the rabbit as a sign that life was multiplying.

Nothing about a tomb.
Nothing about a rock rolling away.
Just bunnies. And babies. And maybe a bonfire.

Painted eggs go back even farther.

Persians, Mesopotamians, and Ukrainians, all had traditions of decorating eggs in springtime. Some used real eggs, others used carved stones or wooden replicas.

In every case, the meaning was clear:
The egg = life.

Not sin. Not salvation.
Just life. Breaking out of a shell. Being born.

(…again, still no Jesus.)

When Christianity started gaining political power, Rome had a decision to make:
What do we do with all these horny, happy pagans?

Simple answer: convert them by compromise.

Keep their holidays.
Just change the meaning.

So Christmas landed on Saturnalia’s turf and absorbed some of the vibe.
Ēostre likely fed into naming Easter.
And the bunny became your child’s pastel-colored sugar dealer.

The old gods were absorbed, not erased. Their symbols were rebranded.

Well, that’s not in Ēostre’s playbook.

The resurrection story, that Jesus was crucified and came back from the dead three days later, became the Christian meaning assigned to the existing spring celebration.

But it wasn’t always celebrated on the same day. It moved around.
Why?

The Church tied Easter’s timing to Passover’s lunar cycle, which happens to follow the same spring equinox rhythms that pagans already used.

So when people say “Jesus is the reason for the season”?
Just smile.

Because you know better now.

The modern Easter you know is a remix.
It’s Jesus meets the Goddess of Spring.
It’s resurrection meets rebirth.

And none of that makes it bad.
It just makes it… human.

This whole book is about that.
Tracing the edits. Finding the fingerprints.

Next up?
We follow the trail back even farther, into the ancient world of many gods and what they taught us before one god stole the spotlight.

sections.title: Chapter Two - Gods Before God
sections.html:
CHAPTER TWO

Gods Before God


BEFORE “IN THE beginning,” there was… everything else.

Long before Christianity, before Judaism, before even monotheism had a name, the world was overflowing with gods. Sun gods, war gods, gods of wine, thunder, love, fertility, fish, corn, harvests, death, dreams, bees, you name it.

Polytheism wasn’t just normal, it was reality.
And in many ways, it still is.

So how the hell did we go from a world full of divine personalities to one bearded guy in the clouds?

We didn’t.

We merged them.

“Pagan” is kind of a slur, honestly. It was a catch-all term early Christians used to describe everyone else.
If you weren’t Jewish or Christian, they’d call you a pagan.

That included the Greek pantheon (Zeus, Hera, Athena, etc.).
The Roman gods (Jupiter, Mars, Venus, literally just renamed Greeks).
The Egyptian gods (Ra, Osiris, Isis, Horus).
The Persian deity Mithras.
Germanic, Norse, Celtic, Slavic, African, and so many others.

These gods were everywhere, because they represented everything.

They weren’t distant abstractions. They were weather, war, childbirth, sickness, and dreams.
The gods lived in rivers, ruled mountains, and showed up in the stars.

And most people believed in lots of them. Not because they were primitive, but because the divine looked like the world: complex, plural, contradictory, alive.

Let’s talk syncretism, a word that should be on the label of every religion sold in bulk.

Syncretism is the merging of different beliefs and mythologies into one. It’s what happens when Ra, the Egyptian sun god, becomes associated with the Greek Helios. Then Sol Invictus in Rome. Then a symbol of Christ, the “light of the world.”

Same sun. New name.

This happened constantly.
Especially under empires, because empires don’t like contradiction.
They want everyone under one umbrella.

So Rome didn’t just conquer people physically.
They conquered their gods.

They’d say:
“Hey, your local god? We know him. That’s just Mercury by another name.”
And just like that, pantheons blurred.

By the time Christianity came to power, the gods weren’t gone.
They were wearing new clothes.

Mithras was a Persian-Roman god whose cult looked, to Christian rivals, suspiciously familiar. Complete with ritual meals, salvation, underground initiation, and cosmic symbolism that echoed later Christian themes.

Saturn was the god of time, agriculture, wealth, and cycles.
Celebrated during Saturnalia, a festival of feasting, gift-giving, and public joy.
Worshipped during the winter solstice.

Sound familiar?

Saturnalia is what Christmas used to be.
When the empire turned Christian, they didn’t cancel the party. They renamed it.

Jesus took the spotlight. Saturn stayed backstage.

Here’s the trick:
Monotheism didn’t replace polytheism.
It repackaged it.

The saints in Catholicism?
They’re basically just gods with job titles.
Saint Christopher protects travelers.
Saint Anthony helps you find lost things.
Saint Valentine handles love affairs.

Each one has a feast day. An icon. And a backstory.

Even Satan, the ultimate villain, borrows from earlier trickster gods and underworld deities.
Lucifer wasn’t even always bad. He was the “morning star,” a poetic reference, later demonized.

This means religion, like language, like culture, like everything, evolves.
And if you follow the trail, you start seeing familiar faces in new masks.

Christianity wasn’t born in a vacuum.
It was born in the ruins and rituals of a thousand older faiths.

It took their symbols. Their stories. Their holidays. Their gods.

It built a new story using old bricks.

And that’s not an insult.
It’s just history.

sections.title: Chapter Three - Hebrew Roots: The Real Old Testament
sections.html:
CHAPTER THREE

Hebrew Roots: The Real Old Testament


YOU WANT TO talk “Old Testament”?
Let’s talk old.

Before Christianity or Paul’s letters, there was the Torah.

And the Torah?
Wasn’t Christian.
Wasn’t Catholic.
Wasn’t Roman.
Wasn’t even written at first.

It was Hebrew.

We’re talking way before churches, pulpits, or printed Bibles.
The stories that would become the Old Testament were oral traditions passed down through generations.

Around campfires.
In exile.
In deserts.
During wars.

And these stories had one job: Keep the identity of a people alive.

Abraham was the first guy who said, “God told me to move.”

Moses was the fugitive-turned-liberator who stood up to Egypt and walked a nation out of slavery.

Real people?
Maybe.
Mythic archetypes?
Absolutely.

The point wasn’t “Was this filmed live?”
The point was “What did it mean for us?”

Let’s get one thing straight:
The Torah isn’t a section of the Bible.
The Bible borrowed the Torah.

The Torah, also called the Pentateuch, is the foundational text of Judaism:

  1. Genesis
  2. Exodus
  3. Leviticus
  4. Numbers
  5. Deuteronomy

It’s not about Christians.
It’s not about Jesus.
It’s not prepping the stage for the sequel.

It’s its own story, with its own laws, culture, symbolism, and struggle. Rooted in the identity of a group of enslaved, exiled, and occupied people trying to make sense of their history and suffering.

And it didn’t call itself “Old.”
That came later, when someone else needed a prequel.

Let’s pause on Moses.
This man is the blueprint.

Raised in Egypt. Kills a guy. Flees to the desert. Hears a voice in a burning bush. Returns to liberate his people. Parts the Red Sea (??). Climbs a mountain. Comes down with the law.

Whether you believe it or not, the story of Moses is the founding myth of liberation theology.

But there’s a catch.

None of this was ever about Jesus.

There’s no mention of Christ.
No passage describes a future figure dying to atone for humanity.
No virgin birth.
No heaven or hell as we know them.
No crosses.

The Torah isn’t about salvation from sin.
It’s about surviving empire.

Did Moses really part the Red Sea?
Did God really create the world in six 24-hour days?
Did Noah really build a floating zoo?

Here’s the trick: You shouldn’t be taking it literally.

Even within Jewish tradition, much of the Torah is understood allegorically.
It’s layered. Symbolic. Mysterious.

The Christians who later insisted on literal interpretation?
They missed the point entirely.

Because metaphor wasn’t a weakness.
It was the whole power.

It let the Torah speak across time.
To refugees.
To warriors.
To the brokenhearted.
To rebels.

Judaism is not Christianity with the Jesus parts removed.
It is a full, self-contained worldview that has its own calendar, its own sacred language, its own laws (613 commandments, not 10), its own festivals (Passover, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur), and a totally different idea of God.

Jews don’t believe in Original Sin.
They don’t believe in the Christian version of hell.
They don’t think a guy needs to die to save the world.

They believe in relationship.
In covenant.
In justice, land, exile, and return.

So how did this sacred text of a small Middle Eastern tribe become the first half of a Roman-approved religion?

Simple: It got reframed.

By the time the New Testament authors started writing (50–120 CE), they were not eyewitnesses, not Hebrew scholars, and mostly writing to Greek-speaking converts.

They needed credibility.
So they reached back into the Hebrew tradition and started saying:
“See? Look here. It said Jesus was coming.”

They took Jewish scripture and used it to validate a brand-new message that Judaism itself explicitly rejected.

Imagine someone turning your diary into fanfiction, and then telling you it’s now canon.

The Old Testament isn’t Christian.
It wasn’t pointing to Christ.
And it didn’t need to be “completed.”

It was a living, breathing framework for a community that had already endured slavery, war, exile, genocide, and empire.

It didn’t need a new savior.

It needed the old stories to keep speaking.

And they still do.

But only when we stop pretending they were a prequel to someone else’s movie.

sections.title: Chapter Four - Jesus Wasn’t a Christian
sections.html:
CHAPTER FOUR

Jesus Wasn’t a Christian


LET’S GET THIS straight:

Jesus of Nazareth was not a Christian.
He never said the word Christian.
He never founded an institution or told people to build a religion.
He wasn’t handing out Bibles.
And he definitely wasn’t preaching Easter bunnies and Christmas trees.

He was a Jewish mystic, teacher, and revolutionary who pissed off both empire and clergy enough to get nailed to a cross.

And what’s wild?

Everything he actually said gets ignored by most people claiming his name.

The term Christian didn’t even show up until decades after his death.

And it was originally an insult.
People in Antioch used the word ‘Christian’ as an outsider jab. Not as a compliment, but as a warning: “Watch out for these weirdos.”

There was no cross necklace.
No hymnals.
No pews.

Just a bunch of outcasts, outlaws, fishermen, and former zealots trying to keep the fire alive.

You know what Jesus actually preached?

“Love your neighbor as yourself.”
“Feed the hungry. Clothe the poor.”
“The kingdom of God is within you.”
“The last will be first, and the first will be last.”
“Blessed are the peacemakers.”
“Turn the other cheek.”
“Forgive seventy times seven.”

That’s it.
That’s the guy.

No threats of hell.
No demands for worship.
No “Accept me or burn.”

Just radical love, scandalous grace, and holy defiance of the systems that crushed people.

He called out corrupt priests.
He flipped tables in temples.
He defied sabbath expectations to heal people.

He broke the rules to remind people what the rules were actually for.

Jesus wasn’t trying to “save your soul.”
He was trying to liberate people’s lives.

He healed the sick.
He touched lepers.
He ate with prostitutes and tax collectors.
He called out hypocrisy.
And he refused to bow to political or religious authority.

He wasn’t trying to start a religion.

He was trying to reclaim a relationship.
Between people and the divine.
Between justice and mercy.
Between each other.

You know what Jesus didn’t say?

That he was “God incarnate.”
That his death would atone for sin.
That you had to “accept him” to be saved.
That his followers should build cathedrals or popes or holy wars.

Those came later.

The virgin birth?
Not in the earliest gospel.
The trinity?
Not mentioned by him.
Hellfire judgment?
Mostly Paul, not Jesus.
“I am God”?
Never said it. Ever.

The gospels were written decades after Jesus died by later believers, not Jesus and almost certainly not eyewitnesses.

They added Old Testament “prophecies” retroactively.
They adjusted timelines.
They even created entire scenes (like the nativity) to match messianic expectations.

Jesus never said, “Start a religion.”
He said, “Follow me.”

And we turned that into:
“Worship the institution that misquoted me.”

Here’s the irony:

If Jesus walked into most churches today, he’d be called a heretic.

If he challenged religious leaders, he’d be excommunicated.

If he stood with the outcast, the undocumented, the queer, the sick, the poor, he’d be labeled “unchristian.”

And that’s because we turned a rebel into a mascot.
A mystic into a monument.
A radical into a ritual.

What did he probably actually want?
For us to love each other.
For us to heal instead of harm.
For us to stop pretending we’re better than others.
For us to stop using God to justify our cruelty.

“Not my will, but yours be done.”
“The kingdom is within you.”
“Go and sin no more.”

He wasn’t handing out Bibles.
He was teaching people how to live.

And he never called it Christianity.

For us to stop using God to justify our cruelty. “Not my will, but yours be done.” “The kingdom is within you.” “Go and sin no more.” He wasn’t handing out Bibles. He was teaching people how to live. And he never called it Christianity.

sections.title: Chapter Five - The Messiah Checklist (And Why He Didn’t Fit)
sections.html:
CHAPTER FIVE

The Messiah Checklist (And Why He Didn’t Fit)


LET’S BACK IT up.

Before Jesus, the Jewish people had a very specific idea of what the Messiah, the “anointed one,” would be like.

Spoiler:
Jesus didn’t check the boxes.

He was many things. Healer, mystic, rebel, and teacher. But the Messiah they were waiting for?
Not quite.

Let’s look at the job description. According to Jewish tradition, the true Messiah would:

  1. Be born of human parents (descendant of King David through his father’s line)
  2. Be a powerful military leader
  3. Rebuild the temple in Jerusalem
  4. Unite all Jews back in Israel
  5. Establish world peace
  6. Restore Jewish law and sovereignty
  7. Usher in the Messianic Age

Not symbolic peace.
Not inner peace.
Literal geopolitical transformation.

A warrior-king. A liberator. A new David.

Human parents?
Nope. Virgin birth.
Military leader?
Not even close. “Turn the other cheek.”
Rebuild the temple?
No temple. And it was later destroyed.
Unite Jews in Israel?
The diaspora spread wider.
Establish world peace?
The Romans crucified him.
Restore law and sovereignty?
He was accused of breaking the law, even as he reinterpreted it.
Messianic Age?
Still waiting, apparently.

They tried.

Matthew and Luke both list different genealogies for Jesus.
Neither makes sense.

Matthew traces him through Joseph, who isn’t his biological father.
Luke contradicts Matthew and doesn’t fit Jewish lineage requirements.

If Jesus is “God’s son,” then he has no bloodline to David.
And if he is Joseph’s biological son, then the whole virgin birth story collapses.

Either way:
Prophecy not fulfilled.

So why did peoples say he was?

Simple answer:
Retroactive editing.

Decades after Jesus died, writers began threading his story into the old prophecies. Massaging the details and reshaping the narrative.

Born in Nazareth?
“Well, he was born in Bethlehem because of a census!”

Poor and executed?
“Well, he suffered just like Isaiah said!”

No royal bloodline?
“Well, Joseph technically descended from David!”

Early writers reframed older prophecies around Jesus’ story.
If the timeline didn’t work, they created a new one.

His followers felt his power.
They believed in his message.
They saw how he healed, loved, and challenged the system.

But their tradition required the Messiah to check the boxes.

So the only way to protect his memory, and make sense of his brutal execution, was to elevate him from rabbi to redeemer.

The shift happened fast.

First he was a teacher.
Then a prophet.
Then the Messiah.
Then the Son of God.
Then God Himself.

And the more divine he became, the more they had to retrofit the past to match the future.

You don’t crucify a peasant.
You martyr a Messiah.

And to do that, you edit the checklist until he fits the frame.

This part matters.

Modern Jewish scholars, and Jewish people for thousands of years, have rejected Jesus as the Messiah not because of hate or blindness, but because he didn’t fulfill the requirements.

Not metaphorically.
Not spiritually.
Literally.

And if your belief system requires metaphors to fill in prophecies, it may be time to re-check the blueprint.

sections.title: Chapter Six - Wait… So Who Wrote This?
sections.html:
CHAPTER SIX

Wait… So Who Wrote This?


FIRST QUESTION: DID Jesus write anything?

Nope.

Not a letter.
Not a scroll.
Not even a diary entry.

The man at the center of the world’s biggest religion?
Never wrote a word of it.

Then where did the stories come from?

The New Testament, specifically the Gospel, is a collection of stories written by other people, decades after Jesus died.

They almost certainly weren’t eyewitnesses.
They didn’t walk with him.
They didn’t take notes in real time.

They were fans.
Followers.
Secondhand collectors.
Sometimes just scribes compiling oral tradition.

Jesus likely died around 30–36 AD.
The earliest Gospel? Mark, written around 70 AD, so ~40 years later.

Mark: 70 AD
Matthew: 80-90 AD
Luke: 80-95 AD
John: 90-120 AD

Let that sink in.
The earliest account of Jesus’s life was written decades later.
After the destruction of the Temple in 70 AD, in a different language, by people who weren’t there.

People didn’t write stories down immediately in the ancient world.
They told them, retold them, and tweaked them.

They made the hero’s entrance more dramatic.
They added symbolism to events.
They cleaned up contradictions.

What started as memory became myth.

Not always maliciously.
Sometimes just because that’s what humans do.

We know because we have the receipts.

Matthew and Luke clearly copied from Mark. Word-for-word in many places.
They contradict each other in details like genealogies, timelines, and locations.
John is radically different. A mystical gospel written last, where Jesus now speaks in long philosophical monologues, unlike the short sayings in the earlier gospels.

These aren’t coordinated eyewitness testimonies.
They’re retellings.

So why four gospels? Why not just one?

Because not everyone agreed on the story.

There were dozens of gospels circulating in the early centuries.
Gospel of Thomas, Gospel of Mary, Gospel of Judas, Gospel of the Hebrews, but only four made the final cut.

Why?
Because church authorities eventually standardized the canon.

We’ll get to that soon.

Each Gospel writer had a different agenda.

Mark was in a hurry. Fast-paced and minimalist. Jesus is misunderstood and abandoned.
Matthew wants to prove Jesus is the Jewish Messiah. Lots of Old Testament callbacks.
Luke is writing for Gentiles. He focuses on compassion and inclusion.
John is pure theology. Jesus isn’t just the Messiah, he is God.

Each version is shaped by the writer’s location, culture, theology, and time period.

This isn’t journalism.
This is theology through storytelling.

So wait… the most influential book in history wasn’t written by its main character?

Correct.

Jesus was a preacher.
A protester.
A radical healer and mystic.

The Bible was written about him, not by him.

And when you understand that, everything changes.

sections.title: Chapter Seven - Constantine and the Council of Nicaea
sections.html:
CHAPTER SEVEN

Constantine and the Council of Nicaea


IN 312 AD, Constantine claimed to see a vision of a cross in the sky before battle, a sign from the Christian God.
He won.
And suddenly, the Roman Empire went from killing Christians to embracing Christianity.

By 325 AD, Constantine wasn’t just tolerating Christianity.
He was shaping it.

Constantine summoned over 300 bishops from across the empire to the city of Nicaea.
Why?
The church was divided.
There were dozens of Christianities.
Some said Jesus was divine.
Some said he was just a man.
Others weren’t even sure he resurrected at all.

It was chaos.
Constantine wanted unity. Not for theology, but for empire.

So he called the first global church council to settle the debate.

The central question:
Is Jesus God?

Arius (a priest from Alexandria): “No, he’s divine, but not equal to God. He was created.”
Athanasius (his opponent): “Yes, he is God, the same as the Father. One essence.”

This wasn’t just philosophy. It was political.
If Jesus wasn’t God, the whole foundation of the new imperial church would shake.

The council sided with Athanasius.
They drafted the Nicene Creed, declaring:

“We believe in one Lord Jesus Christ… begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father…”

And just like that, Jesus’ divinity was officially defined and standardized.

Not metaphorically.
Not mystically.
Canonically.

A lot changed after Nicaea.
The church gained imperial power.
Bishops became political figures.
The bishop of Rome began evolving into the Pope.
Christianity fused with Roman structure. Hierarchy, rituals, holidays, and all.

And perhaps most importantly?

A decentralized spiritual movement became a centralized imperial religion.

So… was Jesus God before Nicaea?

Not officially.
Not universally.
Not doctrinally.

Until Nicaea, the exact nature of Jesus’ divinity was still an open question.

sections.title: Chapter Eight - The Birth of the Bible
sections.html:
CHAPTER EIGHT

The Birth of the Bible


FIRST, LET’S GET something straight. The Bible is not one book.

It’s a library of 66 separate books (more or less, depending who you ask), written by dozens of different authors, across centuries, in different languages, on different continents, with wildly different agendas, and later compiled into a single canon.

And who decided what made it into that canon?

Not God.
A committee.

The “approved” Bible was built in stages, over centuries.
The Council of Carthage in 397 AD was one of the first councils to list the full canon, but different Christian communities continued debating the list for centuries.

The version that stuck, the “Protestant 66,” includes 39 books in the Old Testament (mostly adapted from Hebrew texts) and 27 books in the New Testament (all chosen after Jesus was dead).

This was the final, clean list. “God’s official word,” according to the ruling powers.

But here’s the kicker:

There were dozens of other books floating around. Some more popular than the ones that made it.

So what happened to those?

They got cut.

The Book of Enoch is a trippy, apocalyptic journey filled with angels, giants, and fallen watchers.
Quoted in the Book of Jude.
It was excluded from most canons, partly because it wasn’t universally accepted.

The Gospel of Thomas isn’t a story. It’s a collection of Jesus’s actual sayings.
No birth. No resurrection. No crucifixion.
Just raw, mystical wisdom.

“The Kingdom is inside you and outside you.”

That didn’t fit the church’s narrative.
Cut.

The Gospel of Mary Magdalene portrays Mary as a trusted teacher.
Says Jesus gave her special insight.
Shows the male disciples being jealous.

“The Savior loved her more than the rest of the disciples.”

Uh-oh. That challenged too much power.

Definitely not in.

Who made these decisions?

It wasn’t Jesus.
Or his disciples.
Or the Holy Spirit.

It was church authorities, decades, often centuries, after these texts were written.
Some texts were removed because they didn’t line up with official doctrine.
Others were deemed “dangerous,” “esoteric,” or “heretical.”
And some were just too empowering. Too mystical. Too human.

The message was clear:

If it didn’t serve the centralized narrative, it didn’t make the book.

Apocrypha means “hidden” or “obscure.” These books were part of the Catholic and Orthodox tradition but were removed from the Protestant Bible.

Examples include Tobit, Judith, Wisdom of Solomon, and 1 and 2 Maccabees.

Why were they cut?
Because Martin Luther challenged their authority, and later Protestants removed them.

When someone says, “I believe in the Bible.”

The natural question is:

Which version?
Whose edits?
Which cuts?

Because the “Word of God” was filtered, curated, and canonized through centuries of politics, power, and preference.

What we’re left with is not the full story.
It’s the approved story.

sections.title: Chapter Nine - The Invention of Christianity
sections.html:
CHAPTER NINE

The Invention of Christianity


WHEN CONSTANTINE EMBRACED Christianity in the early 4th century, it wasn’t out of some miraculous conversion at the foot of the cross.
It was a political power move.

Rome was fragmenting. Paganism was losing its grip. Civil unrest was climbing.
What Constantine saw in the fractured Christian cults was a tool.

Something that could unify the empire under a single symbol.
Something that could control the masses without swords.

So in 313 AD, he legalized Christianity.
In 325 AD, he standardized it at the Council of Nicaea.
And by 380 AD, under Emperor Theodosius, Christianity was the official religion of the Roman Empire.

The cross replaced the eagle.
The pulpit replaced the senate.
And Jesus Christ became the imperial brand.

“Catholic” means universal.

The Church wasn’t just preaching anymore. It was ruling.
It became a government body, complete with laws, taxes, land, wars, courts, and kings.

And it wasn’t just Rome anymore.
The Church outlived Rome and later helped legitimize the Holy Roman Empire. A strange beast that was neither fully Roman, nor truly holy.

Religion became empire.
Empire became God.

As the Church rose to power, one position emerged as supreme:

The Bishop of Rome, eventually known as the Pope.

The idea was simple:

“Peter was the rock of the church. He died in Rome.
Therefore, his spiritual authority passed on… to me.”

The Pope became the spokesperson of God.
Later, they would even claim infallibility. The belief that when the Pope speaks on spiritual matters, he cannot be wrong.

You heard that right:

God’s opinion… outsourced to a guy in a hat.

The Church developed a full-on power structure of Popes, cardinals, archbishops, bishops, priests, and peasants.

They controlled education, history, holidays, and salvation itself.

You couldn’t get into heaven without their blessing.

They taxed.
They crowned kings.
They started wars.

They wrote the rules and then sold you the cure for breaking them.
(See: indulgences.)

Want to read the Bible?
Too bad. It’s in Latin. Only priests could read it.
You had to pay to confess, bury your dead, and get married.

And if you questioned it?

Heretic.
Burned.
Tortured.
Forgotten.

When people say, “Christianity is about Jesus,” they’re skipping 400 years of imperial branding and doctrinal editing.

Jesus never said “start a church.”
He never crowned a pope.
He never asked for cathedrals, creeds, or cash.

The religion we now call Christianity wasn’t invented by fishermen or prophets.
It was invented by emperors, bishops, and lawmakers.

sections.title: Chapter Ten - The Protestant Split
sections.html:
CHAPTER TEN

The Protestant Split


1517 WAS THE spark that lit the fire.

The Catholic Church had gotten greedy.

Selling indulgences, hoarding gold, controlling salvation.
It stopped looking like a church and started looking like a bank with incense.

Then came Martin Luther.

A German monk who wasn’t trying to leave, just trying to clean house.
He nailed his 95 Theses to the church door in Wittenberg:
A public “Hey, can we talk?”
The answer was no.

Luther didn’t want to burn down the Bible.
He wanted to burn down the corruption around it.

So he introduced a radical idea:

You don’t need a priest to talk to God.
You don’t need Latin to read the truth.
The Bible is enough.

That’s sola scriptura, “Scripture alone.”

Authority didn’t come from the Pope.
It came from the pages of the book.

It was spiritual revolution through literacy.

Here’s the catch:

Luther cut out the middleman, but not the manuscript.
The Bible he was holding was still the one canonized by the Catholic Church.
Same gospels. Same edits. Same omissions.

All they really did was switch the packaging.

They ditched the Pope, kept the book, and called it freedom.
But the foundation still had Rome written all over it.

Luther’s spark spread like wildfire.
Soon, others were rebelling too. Calvinists, Anglicans, Puritans, and eventually Baptists, Methodists, and Quakers.

Each one tweaking the script.
Each one claiming they’d gotten it right.

And each one still anchored to a canonized Bible.
Chosen by the same bishops they’d rejected.

Protestantism was a break, but it wasn’t a reset.
It rebranded the Church, but didn’t question the source.

They said no to the robe, but yes to the red letters.
They tore down the Vatican, but not the verse.

The control structure got new spokesmen.
But the script stayed mostly the same.

When people say,

“I’m not religious. I’m just spiritual. I just follow the Bible.”

They don’t realize they’re quoting Constantine’s editors.
Not Jesus.

The Protestant Reformation was brave, but incomplete.
They left the gate.
But never checked who built the fence.

The Protestant Reformation was brave, but incomplete. They left the gate. But never checked who built the fence.

sections.title: Chapter Eleven - Evangelicalism: The New Literalists
sections.html:
CHAPTER ELEVEN

Evangelicalism: The New Literalists


THE PROTESTANT SPLIT opened the door.
Evangelicalism walked right through it and slammed it shut behind them.

They weren’t just reading the Bible.
They were worshipping it.

They didn’t just see it as sacred.
They saw it as infallible. Every word, every verse, unedited, untouched, and divine.

Irony alert:
This was still the same canonized manuscript shaped by the imperial church Constantine empowered.
Now treated as if it were dropped from the clouds.

Evangelicalism in America didn’t evolve gradually.
It exploded.

Tent revivals. Fire-and-brimstone preaching.
Sunday school programs teaching five-year-olds that the Earth is 6,000 years old.

Literal six-day creation.
Literal talking snake.
Literal global flood.

And if you questioned it?

You weren’t just wrong.
You were dangerous.

The Bible wasn’t a conversation starter anymore.
It was the final word.

In the U.S., faith fused with nationalism.

Christianity became more than a religion.
It became a brand. A political identity.
A flag-wrapped pipeline from Bible study to ballot box.

Evangelicalism stopped being about spirit.
It became about certainty.

Not faith in the unseen, but belief in being right.

Where Catholicism built a hierarchy of men in robes, Evangelicalism built a hierarchy of ideas.
You must believe Jesus is God.
The Bible is the literal Word of God.
The world is fallen, and only believers are saved.
Doubt is sin.
Questions are weakness.

There’s no room for nuance, history, or edits.
It’s all or nothing.

And in their eyes?
They chose all.

When someone says:

“The Bible is 100% true, word-for-word,”

Ask them:

“Which version?”

They probably don’t know it was shaped and preserved by the imperial church.
They probably don’t know how much was left out.
They probably don’t know Jesus never asked for any of this.

Evangelicalism didn’t rescue Christianity.
It radicalized it.

A religion born in rebellion
Now chained to the very book its founders once questioned.

sections.title: Chapter Twelve - The Bible Isn’t the Enemy
sections.html:
CHAPTER TWELVE

The Bible Isn’t the Enemy


LET’S GET ONE thing straight:
This book isn’t anti-Bible.

We’re not here to burn it.
We’re here to unbury it.

Because under all the edits, the politics, and the theological tampering,
there’s something real in there.

Something human.
Something ancient.
Something true.

It’s just… buried beneath 2,000 years of spin.

The Jesus in the Bible, when you strip away the marketing, isn’t the CEO of a megachurch.

He’s a mystic. A teacher. A radical.

He challenged power, flipped tables, and healed the broken.
He told people to love their enemies.
To forgive.
To serve.

He washed feet. Not for spectacle, but for humility.
He didn't seek a throne.
He warned against religion becoming business.

And then the system he warned about… used his name to build the very thing he came to disrupt.

Not everything in the Bible is literal.
It was never supposed to be.

It’s myth, history, poetry, and proverb.
It’s metaphor, and that’s not a weakness. That’s power.

Because metaphor reaches where facts can’t.
It lets the reader find themselves in the story.

Adam and Eve weren’t just two people in a garden.
They’re a parable of consciousness.
Of temptation.
Of shame.

The stories weren’t just documenting events.
They were decoding existence.

If you read the Bible as a rulebook, it will control you.
If you read it as a mirror, it might awaken you.

Yes, it’s been manipulated.
Yes, it’s missing pieces.
Yes, it’s been weaponized.

But if you know that going in?
You can read it with eyes open.

Not as a slave to doctrine,
but as a seeker of truth.

Jesus never wanted to be a brand.
Or a doctrine.
Or a bullet point on a campaign flyer.

He wanted people to wake up.
To remember who they are.
To live like love actually matters.

Maybe the real blasphemy was turning a mystic into a mascot.

And maybe the redemption is remembering who he really was.

sections.title: Chapter Thirteen - Frankenstein Faith
sections.html:
CHAPTER THIRTEEN

Frankenstein Faith


SO WHAT DO you get when you mix pagan gods, Jewish scripture, Roman politics, Greek philosophy, Middle Eastern mysticism, imperial control mechanisms, and a wandering healer who just wanted people to be kind?

You get Christianity.
Not the man, the machine.

Not Jesus.
The franchise.

Christianity wasn’t born in a manger.
It was assembled in a palace.

Edited by bishops.
Funded by emperors.
Enforced by armies.
Marketed by missionaries.

It borrowed festivals and symbols from the pagan world, folded in solstice feasts and ancient fertility rites, carried forward the language of sacrifice, canonized the gospels that fit its agenda, discarded the ones that didn’t, preached forgiveness, and demanded obedience.

And when people started to question it?

It just reinvented itself again.

This isn’t a religion that spread by chance.
It was engineered to survive.

It moved with colonizers.
It scaled with printing presses.
It adapted to kings, presidents, and televangelists.

It sanctified empires.
Blessed wars.
Justified slavery.
Monetized guilt.

And it did all of this while wearing the face of a man who lived in poverty, rode a donkey, and told people to give everything away.

Understanding how it was built doesn’t mean you have to throw it all away.

But it does mean you’re free.

Free to stop pretending this was ever just about God.
Free to question without shame.
Free to hold onto what’s sacred and leave behind what’s not.

Because if the truth really does set you free, then knowing this?

Is holy work.

sections.title: Chapter Fourteen - So What Now?
sections.html:
CHAPTER FOURTEEN

So What Now?


YOU’VE SEEN THE seams.
The edits.
The empire behind the altar.

You’ve seen how the “Word of God” was translated, redacted, weaponized, and sold. Stitched together by kings and councils and handed down as gospel.

So what do you do with that?

You don’t have to burn it.
You don’t have to bow to it either.

You just hold it differently.

You stop confusing the structure with the Source.
You stop mistaking the religion for the revelation.
You stop letting institutions mediate what was always meant to be direct.

Because Jesus didn’t hand out Bibles.
He didn’t draw lines in the sand.
He broke them.

He didn’t say,
“Worship me.”
He said,
“Follow me.”

Not into churches.
Not into rituals.
But into presence.
Into compassion.
Into truth.

The Bible was never supposed to be the point.
It was supposed to point.

To something deeper.
To something unspoken.
To something within.

So keep what speaks to your soul.
Leave what doesn’t.
And don’t let anyone sell you a gate to a garden you were born into.

The veil is off.

You’re free now.
